prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse foreground–background layout: large rock faces dominate all five frames at roughly 0.2–1.5 m, while darker gaps between and above them appear farther away, perhaps 1.5–4 m. Across the strip, the nearest surface shifts from rocks on the left and center to a broad rock directly in front, then to rocks on the right, consistent with the camera turning or moving laterally rather than clearly approaching or retreating. Bright regions near the lower edge in frames 2, 3, and 5 indicate surfaces or partly cropped foreground forms within arm’s reach, and the faint hand-shaped region at the bottom of frame 4 is also very near the wearer. The map makes relative distance and occlusion boundaries easier to see than RGB, but its smooth, inconsistent brightness over similarly placed rocks, clipped edge regions, and ambiguous bright patches make metre estimates and inter-object distances unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies one large central mask labeled “bed” in frame 3 and small masks labeled “person” near the lower parts of frames 4 and 5; in the RGB context, the large mask is actually a nearby rock face, so its class label is unreliable. The central mask occupies most of the view from about 0.2–1.5 m away, while the person masks correspond mainly to very close, partly cropped body or hand regions at the bottom edge, likely within arm’s reach of the camera wearer. The masks clarify which visible regions are treated as separate foreground instances and show that those person regions move from lower center-right in frame 4 to the lower-left edge of frame 5, although no complete person, facing direction, gaze, or distance to another person can be recovered. Most rocks, gaps, and occlusion relationships are left unsegmented, and the severe cropping and misclassification make the map unreliable for a complete scene layout.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black across all five frames, so it supplies no detected body or hand skeletons and supports no estimates of posture, facing direction, gaze, reach, or person-to-person spacing. In the RGB and segmentation strips, only small, partly out-of-view hand or body regions appear near the lower edge, and their heavy occlusion likely prevents landmark detection. Consequently, the map cannot confirm whether anyone besides the camera wearer is present, where any person faces, or how human pose changes over time. Its main spatial indication is the absence of reliable pose evidence, despite nearby human-colored segmentation regions in frames 4 and 5, making it unreliable for this sequence.
